A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VLMGuard. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions to the evaluation.

before.justification: V1 reports original detection experiments on LLaVA and Phi-3, including AUROC results, ablations, transfer evaluations, and attack-success measurements.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark evaluations, robustness experiments, ablations, pseudo-label measurements, and computational-overhead results in the main text and appendices.

M1.justification: The centered, singular-value-weighted SVD scoring, pseudo-labeling, and classifier pipeline remain. Section 4.1 changes the classifier from a two-layer MLP with intermediate dimension 512 to a three-layer MLP with dimension 1024. This is a limited architectural revision rather than a new detection framework.

E1.justification: V1's ImageNet-based adversarial meta-instructions and XSTest-based visual jailbreak evaluation are replaced by mixtures using JailBreakV-28K, GPT4V-Caption, VLGuard, MLLMGuard, and MSSBench. V2 additionally evaluates abnormal benign inputs from MMMU and scenarios involving paraphrases, typographic instructions, and detector-targeted attacks.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated comparators including HiddenDetect, ASTRA, LlamaGuard3-Vision, LLaVAGuard, Ovis2-34B, InternVL3-78B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct. GPT-5.4 replaces GPT-4V in the main comparisons, and Appendix G adds GuardRank. The larger-backbone comparison also changes from Perplexity/MirrorCheck to HiddenDetect/ASTRA.

E3.justification: The main protocol changes from fixed-size mixtures at pi=0.01 to benchmark-specific mixtures at pi=0.005, with official or random 80/20 splits. Qwen 7B/72B replaces Phi-3 and LLaVA-13B coverage. Classifier training changes from 50 to 20 epochs, learning rate 0.05 to 0.005, and batch size 512 to 128. Validation becomes 100 labeled samples; new protocols include model-judged attack success and low-FPR detection metrics.

E4.justification: Beyond revised versions of existing layer, score, classifier, and benign-sample-count ablations, v2 adds benign paraphrase robustness, abnormal-input tests, same-source confounder controls, token-position/pooling comparisons, text-only controls, threshold sensitivity, pseudo-label quality, subspace alignment, and adaptive attacks. V1's smaller perturbation-radius sweep is removed; v2's white-box PGD experiment instead targets detector evasion.

E5.justification: Both main results tables report averages over five runs and use plus/minus uncertainty entries. V2 applies the same reporting style to additional results without introducing a different run-count policy, seed disclosure, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: Most benchmark and ablation results are replaced under different conditions. For example, v1 reports 92.87 AUROC for LLaVA's meta-instruction average; v2 Table 1 reports averages of 93.00 for LLaVA and 94.79 for Qwen on new benchmark mixtures. New findings include 91.06 AUROC in the same-source control and 95.65/82.36 under typographic/white-box attacks. These are not same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: V2 adds Proposition 3.3 and Appendix K's covariance decomposition, alignment condition, top-k score-gap theorem, and proofs, substantially extending v1's mathematical definitions and intuitive SVD rationale. Definition 2.2 also changes maliciousness from prompts producing malicious outputs to an intention-based latent label and explicitly defines detection risk.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains malicious-prompt detection through unlabeled-data bootstrapping. V2's abstract and introduction add explicit robustness claims for lexical/syntactic variations and emphasize theoretical justification. The headline improvement changes from 13.21 percentage points over Perplexity to 5.39 over GPT-5.4 under different evaluations; the general superiority claim remains.

C2.justification: Section 3.3 introduces the explanation that classifier training suppresses nuisance variations missed by projection scoring. The layer interpretation changes from stronger upper-layer features on LLaVA to stronger intermediate-layer features on Qwen. V2 addresses v1's typography and distribution-shift limitations experimentally and adds substantive qualifications about benchmark-defined maliciousness, context-dependent labels, false positives, and deployment as one layer of defense.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-access link, dataset-count tables, validation-selection criteria, extensive baseline prompts, adaptive-attack settings, and deployment-mode explanations. Appendix J adds measured latency and memory overhead. The reported environment changes from Python 3.8.5/PyTorch 1.13.1/A6000 to Python 3.10.19/PyTorch 2.6.0/A100.

R1.justification: Section 5 substantially revises positioning around multimodal safety benchmarks, dedicated guard models, and activation-based detectors such as HiddenDetect and ASTRA. It expands distinctions from related representation/SVD approaches while removing much of v1's out-of-distribution-detection discussion and citations. These changes exceed bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The introduction, problem formulation, method exposition, experimental narrative, and related work undergo extensive rewriting. V2 reorganizes the classifier discussion into a dedicated Section 3.3, moves qualitative analysis into Appendix B, and restructures the supplementary material. The title, author information, and terminology also change.

P2.justification: V2 retains the original projection sketch within an expanded three-panel Figure 2, reorganizes robustness and ablation plots, replaces qualitative displays, and redesigns the main comparison table with method categories and independent-detector groups. Numerous appendix tables and a threshold plot are added. The journal template also changes typography, headers, and author layout.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical support beyond v1's narrow optimization-based attacks, directly addressing its stated typography and distribution-shift limitations. Adaptive attacks, same-source controls, pseudo-label audits, and deployment metrics provide important checks on practical reliability. These gains outweigh the loss of earlier threat-specific results. Qualifications remain: some label-free wording conflicts with the disclosed labeled validation set, and Appendix K analyzes unweighted projection energy rather than directly proving properties of the implemented weighted score.
